newsitem.title: INDIA: India shares adrift, at mercy of political winds.
newsitem.headline: India shares adrift, at mercy of political winds.

text.p: Indian shares fell on Saturday as bickering politicians tried to stitch together a new coalition and avert snap polls after the United Front government was defeated in a confidence vote overnight, brokers said.
Investors were jittery at the beginning of special trading sessions arranged to give them a chance to react to Friday night's confidence vote.
But brokers said the market had already largely discounted the government's defeat and there was no panic selling.
The benchmark Bombay Stock Exchange's top-30 share index closed 44.01 points, or 1.21 percent, lower at 3,589.72 -- off its 3,574.26 bottom.
The market was held together by hopes a widely welcomed budget would be approved and a new coalition would take over.
The Congress party said it will back the United Front to form a new coalition provided it changed its leader, defeated prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
Prashant Purker, head of institutional sales at Peregrine Capital India, said the market was already largely discounting the optimistic scenario, of a passed budget and new coalition.
Congress party chief Sitaram Kesri told Reuters in New Delhi that his party's top priority was to avoid elections after Deve Gowda's minority government lost the confidence vote.
Analysts saw a glimmer of hope for the markets if elections were avoided.

Tushar Sarda, president and chief executive at Daewoo Securities said he foresaw a good chance of Congress and the United Front together forming a government, in which the parties to the left of the outgoing coalition would drop out.
The left parties were primarily opposed to liberalisation and without them the process of reform will move at a much faster pace, he said.
"It is a hope-driven market," said Ramakrishna Iyer, equity salesman at brokerage ASK-Raymond James Securities India Ltd. "The market will stay in trading range of 100 points."
At 0710 GMT, the 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) index was down 53.34 points, or 1.47 percent, at 3,580.39.
The National exchange index was 13.70 points, or 1.35 percent, lower at 999.70. The Calcutta share index was up 2.73 points, up 2.71 percent, at 103.30.
A consensus agreement among politicians to see through a widely-acclaimed budget also gave investors hope, analysts said.

The speaker of the Lok Sabha (lower house of parliament) has fixed a three-day debate between April 21 and 23 to approve the tax and tariff cutting budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March), held hostage by the political crisis.
"There's an across-the-board support for the budget," Iyer said. "It will rejuvenate the markets if it's passed without significant changes."
He said if the budget was cleared the market was likely trade between 3,600-3,900 from its current 3,300-3,600 range.
Foreign investors were disturbed by the political developments but will not dump shares, analysts said.
"I don't see a major sell-off," said Bharat Iyer, market strategist at UBS Securities, the investment arm of Union Bank of Switzerland.
He said foreign investors put money into Indian stocks because of the long-term growth story and were unlikely to get out due to short-term political instability.
But fresh purchases would slow until the picture became clearer or till valuations became more attractive, analysts said.
